Rivian Says AI Assistant Will Order Your Coffee and Book Service Trips by 2027

Rivian’s AI roadmap: From calendar sync to coffee runs and automated service

InsideEVs reports that Rivian’s chief software officer, Wassym Bensaid, outlined a series of new AI‑driven capabilities for the company’s in‑house assistant during a recent interview on the *Plugged‑In* podcast. The features, which are still in development, are slated for a broader rollout in 2027.

Confirmed developments

  • Assistant already live – Rivian launched its AI assistant in May 2024 with basic voice commands, Google Calendar integration, and Gmail access added in October 2024.
  • Voice‑first vision – Bensaid reiterated the company’s long‑term goal: “through voice and through AI, you will be able to do everything that you’re doing with your fingers on the screen.”

Reported upcoming features (planned, not yet released)

| Feature | What the assistant will do | Status (as of interview) | |---------|----------------------------|--------------------------| | Coffee ordering | Detect a coffee shop along the driver’s route, place an order, and have the drink ready when the vehicle arrives. | Prototype in testing; slated for 2027 launch. | | Proactive service | Continuously monitor vehicle health, diagnose issues, schedule service appointments, and ensure the service center has required parts before the owner arrives. | Development underway; reliability improvements needed before mass release. | | Full‑vehicle control | Expand voice commands to cover virtually every touchscreen function, reducing the need for manual interaction. | Ongoing integration work; timeline aligns with 2027 rollout. |

> *“What I’m really excited about is the possibility in the future where you can bring your own personal digital ecosystem to the car through these AI integrations,”* Bensaid said on the podcast.

Practical implications for owners

  • Convenience – A coffee order placed automatically could eliminate the need to stop and wait, especially on commuter routes.
  • Reduced downtime – Automated diagnostics and pre‑filled service appointments may cut the time a vehicle spends in the shop.
  • Data privacy – Deeper integration with personal calendars, email, and third‑party services will require robust consent mechanisms and security safeguards.
  • Learning curve – Drivers will need to become comfortable issuing more complex voice commands; early adopters may experience occasional misinterpretations as the system is fine‑tuned.

How to verify the announcement

  • Listen to the original interview – The full conversation is available on Spotify, Apple Podcasts, and the InsideEVs website (see the article’s video embed).
  • Check Rivian’s official communications – Rivian’s newsroom and press‑release archive should later publish formal statements or product‑release timelines.
  • Monitor software update logs – Rivian’s over‑the‑air (OTA) update notes will list new assistant capabilities as they become available.
  • Follow regulatory filings – Any major feature that impacts vehicle safety or data handling may be reflected in filings with the NHTSA or EU type‑approval bodies.

Unknowns and caveats

  • Exact rollout schedule – While Bensaid mentioned “2027,” no specific quarter or model‑level rollout plan was disclosed.
  • Geographic availability – It is unclear whether the coffee‑ordering and service‑automation features will launch globally or initially in North America.
  • Partner ecosystem – The assistant will need to integrate with coffee‑shop point‑of‑sale systems and service‑center inventory databases; the readiness of those partners has not been detailed.
  • Performance metrics – No data were provided on expected accuracy rates for voice commands or diagnostic predictions.

Outlook

If Rivian meets its 2027 target, the AI assistant could set a new benchmark for convenience‑focused EV ownership. The company’s emphasis on “efficiency levers” suggests the service‑automation tools may also lower operational costs, potentially translating into competitive pricing for owners. However, the success of these ambitions will hinge on reliable AI performance, seamless third‑party integration, and clear communication of privacy safeguards.
